title: Snake Atlas
text:
Read the signs
Pain, swelling, puncture marks, bruising, weakness, nausea, or trouble breathing can all be warning signs. Symptoms may change over time, so medical evaluation is important even when the bite looks small.






WarningImportant

title: About the Atlas
text:
The atlas follows a simple path through the snake family tree: Serpentes → family → genus → species. Serpentes is the broad group containing snakes. A family gathers related genera, a genus gathers closely related species, and a species identifies one distinct snake.
The Snake Taxonomy Galaxy begins with Snakes at the center and reveals families, representative genera, and individual species as you select each branch. The Follow This Snake story uses one species as a guide, then expands outward to show its relatives in the same genus.

title: About the Atlas
text:
Where the taxonomy comes from
The visualizations use the project dataset in data/snakes-search-results.csv. Each record supplies a scientific species name, an authority, and a Reptile Database link. Family and genus relationships are derived from the scientific name and the site’s taxonomy mapping; species photographs and common names are retrieved from iNaturalist when available.
Because the dataset does not include measurements such as body length, weight, habitat, or geographic range, the supporting comparisons focus on what the data can document directly: the number of records in a family or genus and the relationships between their names.

About this atlas
This page explains the taxonomy data and visualizations used throughout Snake Atlas.

title: Snakebite First Aid
text:
A suspected snakebite is an emergency. Get professional help right away, keep the person still, and follow instructions from emergency services or a poison center.




     



Step 1


Move away and stay calm


Get out of striking distance without approaching the snake. Sit or lie down and move as little as possible.





      



Step 2


Call emergency services now


Call your local emergency number or poison center, even if symptoms seem mild. Put the phone on speaker and follow the dispatcher’s instructions.





     



Step 3


Keep the person and limb still


Help them rest, and gently support the bitten limb so it stays still and below heart level if possible. Avoid walking or unnecessary movement.





     



Step 4


Remove tight items near the bite


Take off rings, watches, and tight clothing on the affected limb before swelling starts. Do not disturb or put pressure on the bite.





    



Step 5


Do not use harmful treatments


Do not cut the wound, suck out venom, apply a tourniquet or ice, or try home remedies. These actions can worsen injury or delay treatment.





     



Step 6


Notice the snake only if safe


From a safe distance, remember its color, pattern, and size, or take a photo only if this does not bring you closer. Never try to catch or kill it.





      



Step 7


Get to a hospital promptly


Go as soon as possible, preferably by ambulance. Clinicians will assess the bite and decide whether antivenom or other treatment is needed.






Important


This website is educational and is not a substitute for emergency care. Never try to catch or handle the snake. If someone has been bitten, contact emergency services or a poison center now.

title: Continental Species
text:
Africa Asia Europe North America South America Oceania







Common snake species


Click a continent on the map to see five familiar species recorded in that region. The source tracks species presence, not population abundance, so this is not a ranking by how many snakes live there.





Important: The Reptile Database regions are geographic distribution regions. A single snake species can occur in more than one region, so the region totals should not be summed to obtain the global number of snake species.


Source: The Reptile Database, Worldwide Diversity of Reptiles. This chart uses the database’s geographic distribution regions and the accepted snake taxon in the Reptile Database advanced search for Serpentes.
Methodology: Counts represent the number of snake species recorded in each geographic distribution region. Because species can be assigned to more than one region, these values are region-level counts rather than unique global totals.

title: Snakebites
text:
A snakebite is the bite itself; envenoming means venom entered the body. Not every bite causes envenoming, and timely medical care can be lifesaving.







How to read this chart: Labels show the annual estimates. The shaded end of Africa’s bar marks its 435,000 to 580,000 range. Africa counts bites needing treatment, Asia estimates envenomings, and the Americas figure counts reported bites treated in health centers. These measures are not directly comparable, and reported cases may miss bites that never reach medical care.


Sources: World Health Organization, Snakebite envenoming fact sheet; Chippaux, Incidence and mortality due to snakebite in the Americas (2017). Regional values come from different sources and methods, not a harmonized dataset.



If a bite happens

Move away from the snake and keep calm.
Call local emergency services immediately.
Keep the person and the affected limb as still as possible.
Do not cut the wound, suck out venom, or apply a tourniquet.



WHO estimates
The World Health Organization estimates that 5.4 million people are bitten by snakes worldwide each year. Of these, 1.8 to 2.7 million experience envenoming, and 81,410 to 137,880 people die each year.
These global figures and the regional chart estimates are population-level estimates, not a count for any individual country or snake species. Regional values use different definitions and may not be directly comparable.
